nodes.name: Navigation controller (input to speed)
nodes.purpose: Turns mouse, keyboard and joystick input into a target forward speed and a target turn rate, ramps the real speed toward the target and integrates position and heading each update

nodes.name: First-person camera rig
nodes.purpose: Mounts the view at the controlled actor with a stored offset, adds roll and yaw on top of the actor transform and pushes the result to the renderer and the audio listener

nodes.name: Path boundaries, actors and spline travel
nodes.purpose: The walkable world is a graph of convex floor regions joined by oriented edges. Actors either steer freely inside a region (player) or follow a spline to a point on an exit edge (non-player)

nodes.name: Drivable vehicles and vehicle swap
nodes.purpose: Per-vehicle top speed and lean ratio, the handover of navigation limits when the player enters or leaves a vehicle, fuel gauge and the helicopter camera moments

nodes.name: Timed delivery missions
nodes.purpose: Rescue and tow vehicles with a draining fuel gauge, a refill trigger and a finish animation chosen by elapsed mission time

nodes.name: Pedestrian extras and crowd budget
nodes.purpose: Background walkers that follow the path graph, choose gait clips by speed, react to being bumped and are spawned or removed to keep the frame time in budget

nodes.name: Race rules, opponent speed control and hazards
nodes.purpose: Lap counting by waypoint, rival speed control with rubber banding, jump ramps, bump reactions, a timed obstacle that knocks the player aside and engine sound feedback

nodes.name: Scenery squash and character customization
nodes.purpose: Plants and buildings shrink or sink when hit and then vanish, and the roster characters cycle color, hat, sound, move and mood on click

nodes.name: Finale: thrown ammo and the chase
nodes.purpose: Parabolic pizza and donut ammo fired from the helicopter, plus the officer and villain speed rules in the final chase

cards.name: Pointer, key and stick input to target speed
cards.summary: Pointer offset from the screen center, held arrow keys or a joystick all become a target forward speed and a target turn value. A dead zone around the center gives zero, and the value then grows linearly to the maximum at the screen edge.
cards.behavior: Movement is steered by where the pointer sits relative to the center of a fixed control box. The box is the window size, except that full screen forces it to 640 by 480. Vertical offset sets the forward target and horizontal offset sets the turn target. Inside the dead zone both targets are zero. Outside it the target grows in a straight line from zero at the dead zone edge to the maximum at the box edge, so the dead zone is removed from the range and no jump occurs at its border. The acceleration used to reach that target also scales with how far the pointer is from the center, with a floor, so a small push gives gentle speed changes and a full push gives hard ones. Releasing the pointer sets both targets to zero and switches acceleration to the large braking value. Held keys act as a full deflection in that direction and therefore request the maximum target. Plain key presses cut the maximum acceleration to a quarter and the floor to a half, and holding the modifier flag named ctrl in the source restores the full values, so key control feels soft unless the modifier is held. A joystick treats the middle band of both axes as released. A hat or point-of-view direction turns the camera yaw only and does not move the actor. The race world narrows the dead zone to a single pixel so steering is proportional all the way to the center, then restores the default when the race ends.

cards.name: Speed ramp, reverse cap and per-update turning
cards.summary: Forward speed moves toward its target at a fixed rate and is capped when reversing. Turning is not smoothed. Each update turns by the turn value times a small sensitivity, so heading changes per update and not per second.
cards.behavior: Each update reads the clock, converts the elapsed milliseconds to seconds and steps the real forward speed toward the target by acceleration times that time, never overshooting. A speed gap smaller than a tiny threshold is treated as arrived. Position then advances along the current heading by speed times elapsed seconds, so forward motion is frame-rate independent. Reverse speed is clamped to forty percent of the current maximum forward speed. Turning works differently. The shipped default leaves the smoothed turn branch off, so the real turn value simply copies the target and the heading rotates by turn value times a sensitivity of 0.4 degrees each update. At the default turn maximum of 20 that is at most 8 degrees per update, so turn speed depends on update rate. The branch that would smooth turning with an acceleration times 40 exists but stays off with the shipped defaults. The heading rotation flips sign when the surface up vector points down, which keeps steering natural on a flipped surface. A world-wide active flag can freeze all navigation.

constants.unit: world units per second

cards.name: Per-vehicle top speed and limit handover
cards.summary: Every vehicle sets its own maximum forward speed and the shared navigation controller adopts it on entry. On exit the previous maximum returns. The listed values are the effective top speeds, not the controller default of 40.
cards.behavior: The navigation controller is shared by all things the player steers. A vehicle class stores its own maximum forward speed in its constructor. When the player gets in, the previous maximum is saved, the previous actor is parked and unhooked from input, and the controller maximum is replaced by the vehicle value. The acceleration and braking limits are not replaced, so a slow vehicle still accelerates at the shared rate and simply tops out sooner. When the player gets out, the saved maximum is restored and the previous actor is put back at the nearest legal spot beside the vehicle. The base class default of 6 applies only to vehicle classes that never set a value. On foot the maximum comes from the action script at load time and is not visible in this repository. In the final act the controller acceleration and braking limits are multiplied by 30 when that world is built, which makes the helicopter respond almost instantly. Whether the shared controller restores those limits when leaving that world is not verified here. Reverse speed is forty percent of whichever maximum is active.

cards.name: Camera roll that leans into turns
cards.summary: Some vehicles roll the camera in proportion to turn value times current speed. The roll is rounded toward zero to whole degrees and only applies while moving forward.
cards.behavior: Four rideable vehicles and the race actors switch on a roll flag. Each update the roll angle in degrees is the negative of turn value divided by the product of maximum forward speed and a per-vehicle ratio, then multiplied by the current forward speed. A larger ratio means a gentler lean. Reversing or standing still gives zero. The result is stored as a whole number, and the camera is rotated only when the whole number changes, so the lean moves in one degree steps and avoids needless camera updates. The roll is applied on top of the stored camera offset, not on the actor, so the vehicle body itself stays level. The ratio for the race car is negative, which flips the lean direction compared with the free-roam vehicles. The dune buggy, rescue vehicle, tow truck and helicopter leave the roll flag off, so they do not lean. As a worked example, the bike at its top speed of 20 with a full turn value of 20 and a ratio of 3 rolls the camera by about 6 degrees.

cards.name: First-person camera mounted above the actor
cards.summary: The view is a stored offset multiplied by the controlled actor transform. The default offset sits 1.25 units above the actor origin and looks straight along the actor heading. Roll and yaw are applied to a copy of the base offset, so they never accumulate.
cards.behavior: When an actor becomes the camera target the rig stores a base transform with the eye at 1.25 units above the actor origin, looking along the actor forward axis with up equal to world up. Every time the actor moves, the rig multiplies this offset by the actor transform and sends the result to the renderer. The same step feeds the audio listener with position, direction, up and velocity, where velocity comes from the change between two view transforms, so Doppler style effects work with no extra input. Roll and yaw requests rebuild the current offset from the stored base every time, which means repeated calls set an absolute angle and not an additive one. When the actor is released the offset is reset to the origin. Scripted moments replace the base. Taking off in the helicopter tilts the offset by 30 degrees about the side axis and landing resets the eye to 1.25 units. At the end of the final act the camera is blended over 3 seconds from the helicopter view to a view that looks straight down from 20 units above a marked point, using an interpolated start and end transform. A hat direction on a joystick sets the yaw to that value in degrees, again from the base offset.

constants.unit: radians (30 degrees), set once at takeoff

constants.unit: world units, set once at landing

cards.name: Convex floor regions with wall sliding
cards.summary: The player moves freely inside a convex floor region. If a step would leave the region through an edge that has no neighbor, the position is clamped onto the wall and slid along it, with a corner case when the hit lands past the end of an edge.
cards.behavior: Walkable space is a graph of convex regions. Each region has edges with outward plane equations. A candidate move is tested against every edge plane, and only planes the new position is behind count. The first plane crossed along the step wins. The code then projects the end position onto that edge and slides along it. If the projection falls before the start or past the end of the edge it clamps to the corner vertex and also checks neighbor edges that face nearly the same way, using a dot product limit, so flat walls made of several short edges act as one wall. When the clamped step ends on an edge that leads to a neighbor region, the region switch runs right after the step and the actor carries on in the neighbor. A step that ends against a wall keeps the actor in the same region. The player is also tested for collision against other actors in the current region and its neighbors up to two regions away, using the swept segment and the actor radius. A hit cancels the step. Because every region is convex, the floor test needs only plane checks per region.

constants.name: plane test epsilon
constants.unit: plane distance units, a point counts as outside when its signed distance is at or below this

constants.name: hit distance tolerance
constants.unit: world units along the step

constants.name: flat wall merge dot limit
constants.unit: dot product of edge normals, neighbors at or below this stop the merge

constants.name: neighbor search depth
constants.unit: regions, collision actors in regions up to this depth are checked

cards.name: Wall hit speed damping and direction nudge
cards.summary: When the player presses into a wall inside the same region, the stored speed is multiplied by 0.8 and the heading is nudged slightly away from the wall. A hit sound is limited to once per second.
cards.behavior: After a step is clamped by a wall and the actor stays in the same region, the code treats it as a wall hit. The controller speed is replaced by speed times the damping value. The default damping is 0.8, so each pressed-in update bleeds twenty percent of the speed. The new position is the clamped slide point. The heading is also nudged by adding a vector from the intended point toward the clamped point, scaled to the heading length times a small factor, which turns the actor gently away from the wall instead of leaving it facing into it. The default factor is about 0.01 and the race car raises it to 0.1 so cars peel off walls faster. A shared sound timer allows the wall sound at most once every 1000 milliseconds. Crossing into a neighbor region is not a wall hit and applies no damping.

constants.name: wall hit speed damping
constants.unit: multiplier on speed, applied each update while pressed into a wall

constants.name: default wall hit direction factor
constants.unit: fraction of heading length added away from the wall, per hit update

constants.name: race car wall hit direction factor
constants.unit: fraction of heading length added away from the wall, per hit update

constants.name: wall sound cooldown

cards.name: Spline travel on the path graph and junction choice
cards.summary: Non-player actors follow a smooth curve from their current pose to a point on an exit edge, then pick the next exit. Speed is in world units per second and the curve parameter advances by speed times elapsed time over curve length.
cards.behavior: An actor that is not steered by the player travels along a cubic curve. Its start pose and heading and its target point and heading define the curve. The target point is a fraction along the exit edge, and both tangent lengths equal the straight distance between start and target, which gives a gentle arc. The duration is stored in a unit chosen so that advancing it by elapsed milliseconds times speed in world units per second produces motion at exactly that speed. The curve is therefore evaluated at traveled distance over duration. Non-player actors start with a reversed start tangent while the player does not. When an actor reaches its target the next exit edge is chosen. The code counts the passable edges around the new region, including the edge just crossed. With one or fewer, the actor takes the first choice. With exactly two, it takes index 1, which is the other edge. With three or more, it asks the actor type. Each named character has its own fixed counting direction and index and a few pick at random. The pedestrian extras have modes. Mode 1 counts counterclockwise and takes index 1, mode 2 counts clockwise and takes index 1, and the default counts counterclockwise with a random index. Path controllers update all their actors from a repeating tick that requests a 10 millisecond interval, with the actual rate unverified. Trigger lines inside a region fire events when an actor crosses them, in either direction.

constants.name: duration scale
constants.unit: converts length in world units to the internal duration, so speed is world units per second

constants.name: path controller tick request
constants.unit: milliseconds between updates requested from the tick manager (actual rate unverified)

constants.name: two edge rule count
constants.unit: passable edge count (entry edge included) at which index 1 is always chosen

constants.name: pedestrian clockwise mode id

capabilities: curve following along a navigation graph

cards.name: Gait clip chosen by speed with distance-synced playback
cards.summary: Each walker owns several movement clips tagged with a speed. The clip used is the first one whose tag is at least the current speed, or the last one when faster than all. Playback time advances with distance, not with the clock, so feet match the ground.
cards.behavior: Locomotion clips are stored in a list sorted by their speed tag. Whenever the actor speed is set, a negative request is clamped to zero, and then the clip index is chosen. If the speed is at or above the fastest tag the fastest clip is used. Otherwise the first clip whose tag is at or above the speed is used, so a slow walker plays a slow clip and a faster one switches to the next gait. The clip time is stepped with the traveled distance, meaning the actor time grows by elapsed time times speed, and the position inside the cycle is that time modulo the clip duration. Because time follows distance, stride length stays constant and feet do not slide on the ground at any speed. When the speed reaches zero a standing actor holds its current pose from the clip cycle. Some special clips use reserved negative speed tags and are never picked by the speed rule. They are looked up by tag for scripted moments such as a kick reaction or a shooting pose.

constants.unit: world units per second, negative speed requests become this

constants.unit: speed tag value, never matched by the speed rule

constants.name: reserved clip tag for the second scripted clip

cards.name: Pedestrian bump: tumble or brick-apart reaction
cards.summary: A pedestrian that walks into the player turns around and ignores the player for 100 checks. When the player drives into a pedestrian, only every second contact reacts. The reaction is a break-apart and rebuild clip when there is room, or a 2 second tumble when there is not.
cards.behavior: Two contacts exist. In the first, a pedestrian walks into the player. It tests the player as a sphere of radius 1 against its movement ray, using the quadratic solution, so a grazing ray counts as a hit. The pedestrian then reverses direction and sets a block counter of 100 checks. While that counter runs and the player is within about 3.2 units, the test is skipped, so the same contact cannot fire again and again. In the second, the player drives into a pedestrian. A global counter lets only every second contact cause a reaction, and the other contacts do nothing. On a reacting contact, a spot 2 units from the pedestrian along the player heading is tested against the region planes. If the spot is inside the region, the pedestrian plays a disassembly clip, freezes at speed zero, then plays an assembly clip and restores its old speed and pose. If the spot is outside, the pedestrian is lifted 2.5 units and rotated by 0.7 radians each update about an axis chosen from the player heading, which tumbles it. After 2 seconds it is set down. Collision is disabled during both reactions, and nothing starts if either actor is not in its normal state. A pedestrian also pauses when its region holds a scene animation and resumes when that ends.

cards.name: Pedestrian count that adapts to frame time
cards.summary: The allowed number of pedestrians starts at 5 and moves between 2 and a cap of 10 or 20 depending on the island quality setting. It goes down when the smoothed frame time is slow and up when it is fast.
cards.behavior: The animation manager keeps a budget for background walkers. At world start the budget is 5. The cap is 10 for the lower quality settings and 20 above them. On a random timer of 5 to 15 seconds the manager tries to add one walker, and only if the stored time of the last scripted event is more than 10 seconds old. Right after, it measures the last frame time. Frame times outside the range 0.01 to 1 seconds are ignored. Valid samples are smoothed by weighting the old average by 2 and the new sample by 1, then dividing by 3. If the raw sample is slower than 0.2 seconds and the budget is above 2, the budget goes down by one. Otherwise, if the smoothed time is under 0.16 seconds and the budget is below the cap, the budget goes up by one. The result is a slow, steady adjustment that fills the island when the machine is quick and thins it when it is not, with no hard switch. The same update can also start a scripted animation with a walker that is in view, ahead of the player inside a cone with a dot product above 0.707, when the player speed is inside a speed window.

cards.name: Fuel gauge that drains and refills at a trigger
cards.summary: Four vehicles show a fuel gauge that drains to empty in 300 seconds and refills when the vehicle crosses the gas station path trigger. In this repository the gauge feeds only the dashboard and does not reduce speed.
cards.behavior: Each fueled vehicle stores a fuel fraction that starts full. While the player drives it, every update subtracts a tiny amount per elapsed millisecond. The rate empties a full tank in 300000 milliseconds, which is 300 seconds, and the value is clamped at zero. The fraction is written to a dashboard variable as text each update, and so is the speed fraction, which is absolute speed divided by the current maximum. A path trigger on the gas station sets the fraction back to 1. In this repository the fraction is read only to build dashboard text. No branch reduces speed, stops the vehicle or ends play when the gauge is empty, so the gauge is a display and a goal for the player and not a limit. The motorcycle, the dune buggy, the rescue vehicle and the tow truck use the same drain rate and the same refill trigger. The jetski publishes a speed fraction only.

constants.unit: fuel fraction per millisecond of wall clock, applied each update (300 seconds from full to empty)

constants.unit: fraction of a full tank

cards.name: Mission result picked by elapsed time
cards.summary: The rescue and tow missions measure the time between start and finish and pick one of three finish animations and score colors from fixed thresholds. The tow mission also plays a nudge voice line after 100 seconds.
cards.behavior: On the final trigger of a mission the game subtracts the start time from the clock. For the rescue mission, after both of its tasks are done, under 300 seconds earns the best result, under 400 seconds the middle one, and anything slower the lowest, and the score color is updated to match. The tow mission uses 200 and 300 seconds. The tow mission also runs a check on every update while the player drives it and the mission is in its started state. After 100 seconds without finishing it plays a reminder voice line once, then sets a flag so it does not repeat. The mission state machine moves through started, hooked up and finished steps, driven by path triggers such as camera animation points, final waypoints and a hookup point. The thresholds are plain differences of the game clock.

cards.name: Rival speed: accelerate to a target, slow in curves
cards.summary: A rival does not use the player controller. Its speed moves toward a target at a fixed rate. The target is cut in curves, and car and jetski rivals use different strengths.
cards.behavior: Each update the rival computes a target speed from its stored maximum. If the absolute dot product of the destination edge face normal and the heading is above 0.5, the target is multiplied by a curve factor. The source names this factor for curves, and the exact edge geometry that triggers it on the shipped track was not verified here. Cars use 0.65, a strong cut. Jetskis use 0.95, a very mild cut. The target then goes through the catch-up rule in the rubber band card. The real speed moves toward the target by elapsed milliseconds times the acceleration value and never passes the target, so up and down changes both use the same rate. The car rate is 0.03 and the jetski rate is 0.04 speed units per millisecond, which is 30 and 40 units per second squared. The rival waits for the race state variable to read racing before it moves. Before the race starts, the rival maximum is captured from the speed value that the script gives it, and that number is not in this repository. The finish state is entered by setting the maximum below zero, which zeroes the speed.

cards.name: Rubber banding from waypoint lead
cards.summary: Rivals slow down when they are two or more waypoints ahead of the player and speed up by 30 percent when they are more than one behind. The lead is counted in waypoint indexes, so it adapts to track position, not distance.
cards.behavior: Every waypoint on the track has an index, and each racer stores the latest one it passed. The rival compares its latest index with the player latest index. If the rival is ahead by one or less, nothing changes. If it is ahead by two, its target speed is cut by a quarter of the rubber band factor times one. If it is ahead by three or more, the lead is capped at three and the cut is the quarter factor times two. With the car factor of 0.6 this gives 85 percent and 70 percent of normal target speed. With the jetski factor of 0.5 it gives 87.5 percent and 75 percent. If the rival is behind by two or more, the target is multiplied by 1.3 for both vehicle types. The effect is a loose elastic band that keeps the race tight without a hard cap. It uses the same speed ramp as normal control, so the change is gradual. Whether the per-actor waypoint index wraps at each lap was not verified here.

cards.name: Laps by waypoint order, progress bar and 1 to 3 score
cards.summary: A lap is 20 waypoints. A waypoint only counts when its index is higher than the last and no more than four steps ahead, which blocks shortcuts. Races last 2 laps. The score is 3, 2 or 1 by how many rivals have fewer laps at the moment the player finishes.
cards.behavior: Each racer reports waypoints from path triggers. The race accepts an index only if it is larger than the last accepted one and less than five above it. This stops a player from skipping the lap by cutting across the infield. Reaching index 20 resets the index and adds a lap. A progress value shown on the dashboard is a fixed offset plus a scale times the lap number times 20 plus the index, divided by the total lap count times 20, so the bar fills smoothly across both laps. The offsets and scales are 0.036 and 0.928 for the car race and 0.032 and 0.936 for the jetski race. The rival markers use the same formula against a pixel box. When the player completes the final lap the score is 3 if both rivals have fewer laps, 2 if only one does and 1 otherwise. The best score is stored per playable character. In the car race, input is disabled and a win or loss scene plays. In the jetski race a rival that finishes its laps has its top speed set to 0.1, so it coasts to a stop.

cards.name: Jump ramps that carry the speed through a launch curve
cards.summary: Crossing a ramp edge switches the racer to a fixed launch curve to a marked landing edge. The speed is raised to at least 8, tangents are five times the unit direction, and the player returns to free steering on landing.
cards.behavior: Ramp edges are listed in pairs. Crossing the first edge of a pair sets the actor to a ready state, lifts its speed to at least 8 if it was slower, and builds a curve from the current position to the middle of the paired landing edge. The player aims at the middle of the target edge. The start tangent is the current heading times 5 and the end tangent is the landing direction times 5, so the arc leaves along the heading and arrives parallel to the landing edge. A rival has its start heading flipped. While the ready state lasts the actor follows the curve and ignores steering. On reaching the end the region is switched to the landing region and the state returns to normal. For the player, the controller speed is set from the carried speed so the landing continues at the same pace. Jetski races use the same scheme with their own edge indexes and the same minimum speed of 8, but their tangents are the plain unit directions.

cards.name: Timed obstacle that knocks the player aside
cards.summary: On one stretch of the car race an animated obstacle swings through the road. If the player is on a hazard region while its animation is inside a short phase window, the player is knocked aside by a camera driven kick animation.
cards.behavior: Six road regions sit under the obstacle. Twelve rows give a region, a window of the obstacle animation phase and a kick side, so each region has two windows. The phase is the playhead divided by the duration. The windows are 0.1 to 0.2, 0.2 to 0.3, 0.3 to 0.4, 0.6 to 0.7, 0.7 to 0.8 and 0.8 to 0.9, so the obstacle sweeps across the road in two passes per cycle. While the player is on one of these regions the game checks the rows every update. A match sets the kick state to side one or side two, plays a sound and starts a camera animation lasting its own duration. During the kick the camera and the car body follow the clip. When it ends the car is placed on one of two fixed regions and normal play resumes. Hazards are therefore dodged by timing, not by speed.

cards.name: Race bump tumble, engine pitch and idle reminder
cards.summary: A racer that hits another is lifted 2 units and spins for 2 seconds. Player engine pitch follows speed with a gear-like saw tooth. Standing still in a race for 5 seconds plays a voice reminder once.
cards.behavior: When a racer hits another and the other is in its normal state, the other is lifted by 2 units and set to a hit state. During the next 2 seconds it is rotated by 0.6 radians each update, which tumbles it. Afterwards it is lowered back and returns to normal. The player is never tumbled. For the player car, the call returns success only when the player caused the hit and is moving, and failure otherwise. A voice line is allowed once every 3 seconds. For sound, the free speed fraction is the absolute speed over the maximum. Above 83 percent of the maximum the pitch factor is a fixed 1.9. Below that, the pitch is 0.7 plus a value that rises from 0 to 1.25 as speed times 6 modulo 100 over 80, which makes the pitch climb and drop like gear shifts. The jetski pitch is a straight line, the speed fraction times 1.2 plus 0.7. If the player speed stays zero for 5 seconds after having moved once, a reminder plays and is not repeated until the player moves again.

cards.name: Plants that sink in steps and wobble when hit
cards.summary: Four plant types have a hit counter of 1, 2, 2 or 3. Each hit drops the plant by a fixed height per step and wobbles it for about a second, and the last hit hides it. The palm takes two hits and the others one in the cited counter logic.
cards.behavior: Every plant has a type, a color from a list of five and a counter that starts unset. The first hit sets the counter to the type value of 1, 2, 2 or 3. A hit subtracts one, and a counter that reaches one is forced to zero, so only the type with 3 survives the first hit. A zero counter hides the plant. Otherwise the plant sinks into the ground by the counter shortfall times a per-type step of 0.1, 0.7, 0.5 or 0.9 units. During the wobble a repeating tick every 50 ms applies a shear on the up axis and a squash with scales 1.03, 0.95 and 1.03. The shear uses sine waves at 2 and 4 cycles per second with an amplitude of 0.2. The wobble runs during the last second before an end time, and that end time is the animation length passed to the schedule call plus 1 second after the hit. Clicking also cycles the plant through its five colors and wraps. The effect is a cheap, readable bash reaction from first person.

cards.name: Buildings that shake and sink when hit
cards.summary: A hit building loses 2 from its counter, shakes up and down at 10 cycles per second with a 0.4 unit amplitude while its base falls 0.05 per update, and then rests at a lower height or disappears at zero.
cards.behavior: Each building has a counter and a per-building drop scale. A hit schedules an end time of the animation length plus one second after the hit. A repeating tick that requests 50 ms drives it, and the shake runs during the last second before the end time. During the shake the building is moved vertically to a sine wave at 10 cycles per second with an amplitude of 0.4 around a baseline, and the baseline falls by 0.05 on every tick, so the building also settles downward. A crash sound is played once with a falloff between 35 and 60 units. The counter is reduced by 2. When the animation ends the building is set to a height from the counter times its drop scale. If the counter reached zero it is hidden. Some calls hide the building when the animation ends regardless of the counter. Counters can be reset to the starting values for a new game.

cards.name: Click-to-cycle character customization
cards.summary: Clicking part of a roster character advances that part to the next option in a ring. Color, hat, sound, move and mood each keep their own index and wrap at a fixed length.
cards.behavior: A roster character has 10 body parts. A click on a part moves a color index along that part own list, which ends at a sentinel value, and wraps to the first entry. A click on a hand or claw acts on the matching arm, a click on the head acts on the hat part and a click on the body acts on the torso part. Parts that do not allow color are skipped. A hat click moves to the next hat shape, copies the mesh set and tints it with the current color. Separate counters pick one of 9 sounds and one of 4 moves, and a mood from 0 to 3. The move index plus a base of 10 selects the animation id. The sound index plus 50 selects a sound, and the mood plus 66 selects a mood sound. All state is stored on the character record so it persists when the model is released and rebuilt, and it is written to the save data.

cards.name: Thrown pizza and donut arcs that land at the aim point
cards.summary: Firing from the helicopter builds a parabola from the camera through the point where the aim ray meets the ground plane. Flight always lasts 1 second. Twenty slots exist for each ammo type and a shot fails when all are in use.
cards.behavior: The shot starts 3 units in front of the camera along the view direction. The code finds where the view ray meets the ground at height zero and fits a quadratic through the start and that ground point, with the launch up direction as the start slope and straight down as the end slope. The projectile then moves along the curve by a parameter that grows with elapsed time. Speed is set to 10 and total length to 10000, so the projectile always takes 1000 milliseconds no matter how far it flies. A path controller then checks which region the curve meets and attaches the shot there, so it can hit actors on the ground. Shots that find no region use a fallback that removes the shot at the end of its flight and plays a hit sound. Pizza models are scaled by 2 and donut models by 5, and their collision spheres are scaled the same. In flight the ammo spins. A hit actor is lifted 5 units and rotated 0.6 radians per update for 2 seconds before it recovers. A failed curve fit returns failure at once.

cards.name: Final chase: officer and villain speed rules
cards.summary: Officers walk at 2 and sprint at 6 for 2 seconds after eating a donut. The villain moves at 5 and slows to 3 for 2 seconds after eating a pizza. Officers replan toward the villain inside 12 units and catch it inside 2 units.
cards.behavior: Both sides use the path graph. Officers start at a base speed of 2. Touching a thrown donut makes the officer eat it, jump to a speed of 6 and replan its route. After 2 seconds the speed returns to 2. The villain moves at 5. Touching a thrown pizza makes it eat the pizza, slow to 3 for 2 seconds, count the pizza and plan a new route. After eight pizzas it stops hunting more and plays a different voice line. Each officer check measures the squared distance to the villain. Under 4, which is 2 units, the chase ends in a win. Under 25, which is 5 units, the villain actor is put in the disabled state and the officer replans. When the squared distance is under 144, which is 12 units, the officer plans a direct path to the villain current position and heading. While hunting, the villain looks at thrown pizzas, and a pizza farther than 40 units from it is handed to a shark instead. Thrown food therefore steers the pursuit. Pizzas slow the villain and donuts speed up the officers.
